title: Neuronal FICD shapes motivated behavior through modulation of dopamine receptor dynamics
authors: Weaver, K. J.; Abdon, B.; Toth, B.; Jack, A.; Giblin, W.; Burgess, C. R.; Pletcher, S. D.; truttmann, m. c.
abstract: Motivated behaviors rely on dopaminergic signaling, which in turn depends on the correct folding and trafficking of receptors through the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Within the ER, the AMPylase enzyme FICD acts as a molecular rheostat through its modification of the chaperone BiP, dynamically tuning the organelle's responsiveness to folding perturbations and cellular stress. While the biochemistry of FICD is well-established, its role in complex animal behavior remains poorly understood. Here, we identify FICD as a conserved contributor to the generation of motivated behavior. In Drosophila, pan-neuronal knockdown of dFic significantly reduces feeding, spontaneous locomotion, and reward-seeking behavior. These alterations occur without disrupting circadian architecture, motor capacity, or homeostatic hunger, indicating a specific loss of motivational drive. Depleting dFic within subsets of dopamine receptor-expressing (Dop1R1) neurons recapitulates these behavioral alterations. Transcriptomic profiling reveals that dFic depletion does not induce a canonical unfolded protein response, pointing to a specific post-transcriptional alteration rather than global ER stress. At the molecular level, dysregulated dFic alters the localization and abundance of Dop1R1. Finally, we demonstrate that this regulatory axis is evolutionarily conserved, as loss of FICD similarly diminishes motivated behaviors in C. elegans and mice. Together, these findings implicate FICD in the generation of motivated behavior and link dynamic control of ER proteostasis to dopamine-receptor maturation.

title: Do LLM Proposers Improve Budgeted Search for Ionizable Lipids?
authors: Singh, H.; SINGH, R. K.; Krishna, C. S.; Srivastava, S. P.; Gorantla, R.
abstract: Efficient lipid design under limited experimental budgets is a central challenge in computational chemistry and drug discovery. We introduce LEAF (Lipid Evolutionary Adaptive Framework), a matched-budget protocol for testing whether language-model proposers improve combinatorial molecular search relative to classical baselines. The study uses a 30,044-candidate ionizable-lipid space, a frozen Gaussian-process oracle fitted to experimental potency labels, and a separate active-learning surrogate. Four language models evaluated over eight seeds and three splits show no significant improvement over genetic-algorithm or random-search baselines. For Llama 8B, 79.1% of acquisition-selected queries repeat previously evaluated archive members. Removing duplicates reduces the performance gap on some splits but increases proposal cost and can prevent budget exhaustion. Larger models reduce duplication without establishing superiority or equivalence. Exploratory scored prompts and stricter novelty controls yield positive median differences against the genetic algorithm, yet wide intervals and shared-seed dependence preclude stronger conclusions. A validated single-assay reanalysis preserves the chemotype-cold deficit at a smaller numerical scale, and exploratory expected hypervolume improvement does not reverse the result. Follow-up checks address whether proposers genuinely use injected evidence. These checks include a zero-shot leakage probe, rank-only and chain-of-thought-rationale prompts, a score-shuffle perturbation, an evidence-conflict probe, and a genuine reasoning-mode proposer. They show measurable engagement with supplied information without a corresponding performance gain. LEAF isolates proposal quality as the experimental variable and documents a concrete failure mode of zero-shot LLM proposers under controlled budgets.

title: BioMod: Biological Module Tokenization for Single-Cell Foundation Modeling
authors: Meng, L.; Zhu, J.; Han, B.; Zang, Y.; Li, W.; Zong, K.; Zhong, J.; Yang, Y.; Liu, J.; Jia, J.; Sun, R.; Yu, G.; Han, J.; Chen, Y.; Zhang, L.; Xu, J.
abstract: Single-cell foundation models typically represent cells as flat sequences of individual genes, requiring higher-order biological organization to be inferred implicitly from sparse expression profiles. Similar to the evolution from character-level to semantic tokenization in natural language processing,we hypothesize that cellular states can be more efficiently represented using biologically meaningful intermediate units. Here we present BioMod, a 50-million-parameter single-cell foundation model that introduces biological modules as representation units between genes and cells. BioMod constructs an overlapping vocabulary of 660 biological modules derived from curated pathways and data-driven gene programs, replacing thousands of gene-level inputs with compact module representations. Pretrained on approximately 73 million human cells using high-ratio module masking with an asymmetric decoder, BioMod achieves state-of-the-art performance across cell-type annotation, zero-shot batch integration, perturbation-response prediction and drug-response forecasting while maintaining a compact architecture that enables efficient inference on a single GPU. Module-level analyses further demonstrate that BioMod captures biologically meaningful cellular programs and preserves pathway-level organization.

title: HERO: A hierarchy-aware analysis pipeline for reducing and refining whole-brain atlas-mapped cellular datasets
authors: Shipman, A. L.; Centanni, S. W.
abstract: Advances in high-throughput mesoscale microscopy and machine learning-based image analysis pipelines have made unbiased whole-brain imaging widely accessible. However, translating the resulting atlas-mapped datasets into biologically meaningful results remains a substantial barrier owing to their sheer magnitude and complex hierarchical organization. Consequently, reporting structure and analysis methods vary widely across studies, undermining rigor and reproducibility. To address this, we developed a user-friendly data reduction workflow, HERO (Hierarchy-aware Expression Region Organization), designed to perform hierarchy-aware selection, refinement, ranking, and visualization of whole-brain cell detection datasets. The workflow is customizable to specific needs, requires minimal coding experience, and outputs transparent, curated results. HERO functions as a seamless plug-in within larger-scale whole-brain cell detection analysis pipelines, providing efficient, unbiased region selection to streamline subsequent statistical analyses and comparative evaluations. Although HERO is developed with mouse cell-detection datasets, it can be applied to any atlas-mapped dataset that contains hierarchical information. Here, we applied the HERO pipeline to example cell detection datasets containing afferent cells from the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST) and the insular cortex (insula). HERO provided top projecting regions consistent with historical tracing studies for the BST (e.g., amygdalar and hypothalamic regions) and the insula (e.g., somatosensory, autonomic, and interoceptive regions). Furthermore, the refinement step of HERO provides additional enriched regions originally obscured in the primary ranked outputs, such as memory- and emotion-associated structures. With HEROs dynamic processing, we were able to identify top-projecting regions consistent with the literature and, additionally, find regions often obscured in these large datasets. In sum, HERO offers a standardized analysis workflow to reduce whole-brain cell-detection datasets, transforming raw regional cell counts into curated results and advancing the effectiveness, interpretability, and accessibility of whole-brain imaging in neuroscience.

title: Criticality-related dynamics accompany long-term functional decline in primary cortical MEA cultures
authors: Escobar, A.; Gil-Bea, F. J.; Rodriguez-Gomez, L.
abstract: Primary cortical neuron cultures are widely used to study network development and decline, but their long-term electrophysiological trajectories are poorly characterized. We used multi-electrode arrays to longitudinally monitor Wistar rat cortical cultures for up to ~730 days in vitro (DIV), combining activity measures with survival analysis and criticality metrics. Wells shared an early developmental phase, with mean firing rate peaking at 12-14 Hz around DIV 100-150, before diverging into two phenotypes: early-death wells, showing progressive loss of burst organization, longer inter-burst intervals, shorter bursts, and steep declines in active-electrode recruitment; and long-survival wells, which sustained organized bursting and measurable activity well beyond DIV 400, in some cases past DIV 700. Cox proportional-hazards modeling with FDR correction across thirteen candidate features identified burst duration, inter-burst interval, synchrony, mean firing rate, branching ratio, and Kappa index as significant predictors of time to network failure. Criticality metrics offered the most mechanistic insight: in early-death wells, branching ratio declined toward zero and Kappa index rose toward its upper bound as networks approached silencing. Beyond their average levels, the rate of change of branching ratio and Kappa index over recordings was the strongest correlate of survival time among all criticality metrics. Neuronal avalanche size and duration exponents and their scaling relation, remained consistent with scale-free dynamics in both phenotypes while networks were active, though avalanche occurrence rate declined progressively in early-death wells without reaching significance as an independent predictor. These results show that long-term network survival is not determined by firing rate alone, but by preserved burst organization, sustained electrode recruitment and near-critical propagation dynamics. This work offers one of the longest electrophysiological characterizations of rodent cortical cultures to date and identifies criticality-based metrics as promising tools for predicting network decline and evaluating interventions to preserve long-term neuronal function.

title: Deciphering auditory neuroprogenitor stemness for large-scale neuronal screening
authors: Rousset, F.; Pepe, L.; Sarhadi, M.; Lemeille, S.; Sgroi, S.; Oberhauser, L.; Daskalou, D.; Ilmjarv, S.; Braun, S.; Senn, P.
abstract: Sensorineural hearing loss can arise from damage to sensory hair cells, auditory neurons or their synaptic connections, with auditory neuropathy and cochlear synaptopathy highlighting the importance of neural integrity for hearing. The mammalian cochlea has limited capacity to regenerate lost auditory neurons. Understanding the molecular programs that sustain cochlear progenitor expansion and neurogenic competence could support neuronal regeneration and provide renewable models for auditory drug discovery. We previously established that WNT activation combined with dual SMAD inhibition (CHIR-DS) supports scalable expansion and neuronal differentiation of mouse auditory neuroprogenitors (ANPGs). Here, we characterize the transcriptional, chromatin and metabolic changes associated with the induced state. RNA-seq and ATAC-seq identified reduced Id1 and Id2 expression and increased accessibility at proneural basic helix-loop-helix motifs, alongside transcriptional enrichment of translation, mTOR and glucose-metabolism programs. Compared with growth-factor controls, CHIR-DS-treated ANPGs showed slight increase in glycolysis at early passage. However, after long-term expansion, both glycolysis and mitochondrial respiration were markedly enhanced. Human fetal ANPGs also responded to CHIR-DS with increased sphere growth and retained neural differentiation capacity, providing proof of concept beyond the mouse system. Finally, neurons derived from stemness-induced ANPGs (siANs) supported a 384-well reporter assay and a 2,560-compound pilot screen that nominated candidate neurite-outgrowth enhancers. Together, these findings validate the pathway basis of ANPG stemness induction, characterize the resulting molecular and metabolic state, and demonstrate human feasibility and a neuronal screening application.

title: A foundation model for brain organoid network dynamics uncovers intrinsic computation and convergent disease phenotypes
authors: Schweiger, H. E.; Robbins, A.; Hernandez, S.; Moreno-Ochando, A.; Cline, I.; Doganyigit, K.; Mouzaya, M.; Hussain, K.; Pang, Z. P.; Duan, J.; Salama, S. R.; Pollen, A. A.; Bhaduri, A.; Haussler, D.; Teodorescu, M.; Mostajo-Radji, M. A.
abstract: Brain organoids develop self-organizing neural networks that can be used to model neurodevelopment and disease. Here we introduce PULSE, a foundation model developed using over 900 hours of high-density microelectrode array recordings of in vitro and ex vivo neural tissue. We show that this single model can address two open questions: how disease-associated variants alter network development, and how naive circuits encode information. PULSE revealed accelerated network maturation in held-out human 16p11.2-deletion organoids. It also revealed a change in network coordination shared with SHANK3 deficiency. Because organoids develop without sensory input, they let us ask how circuits encode information before any representation is learned. Closed-loop control of a virtual inverted pendulum engaged existing spontaneous activity patterns rather than creating new ones. PULSE provides a common reference frame for neural circuits across genotypes, protocols and tasks.

title: Reuse of learned subtask representations during human planning
authors: Seak, L. C. U.; Luettgau, L.; Eckstein, M. K.; Moran, R.; Dolan, R. J.
abstract: The notion of a compositional reuse of previously learned problem solutions predicts that the human brain should reinstate such learned subtask representations during planning. Here, we test this in a value-ranking task implemented in an online and a magnetoencephalography (MEG) experiment, respectively. Participants first learned pairwise rankings and subsequently solved problems where these learned rankings could either be reused or required reordering. Behaviourally, in the online experiment, we show the availability of a reusable subtask structure improved accuracy, with computational modelling indicating a greater weighting of subtask-level value when participants could avail of this learnt structure. In MEG, during planning, we show enhanced reactivation of task-relevant subtask representations in the reusable condition, and particularly so early in the experiment. In a subsequent probe task, we show subtask-identity representations generalised to a novel context and that stimuli belonging to the same learned subtask manifest an increase in their neural similarity. Temporally delayed linear modelling (TDLM) revealed forward and backward sequential reactivation at a subtask level, alongside backward stimulus-level replay, with subtask sequenceness varying according to task context. The findings provide convergent behavioural, computational and neural evidence for reactivation and reuse of learnt relational structures for novel problem solving.

title: Linking anterior cingulate sulcal variability to attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder behavior
authors: Hadveck, R. F.; Paras, A.; Anctil, M.; Martinez, E.; Gallardo, C. M.; Maboudian, S. A.; Willbrand, E. H.; Weiner, K. S.
abstract: Background: The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is consistently implicated in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). ACC variability, including its most variable structure, the paracingulate sulcus (PCGS), has been known since the late 1800s, and since then, has been linked to cognitive control, impulsivity, and psychiatric conditions comorbid with ADHD, including autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia. Yet, the role of the PCGS in ADHD remains unexamined at the individual level. Methods: We characterized PCGS incidence, asymmetry, and morphology in 247 children and adolescents (144 ADHD: 10.9 +/- 2.73 years old, 75% male; 103 neurotypical: 12.2 +/- 3.17 years old, 50% male) from the ADHD-200 dataset. The PCGS was manually identified in FreeSurfer cortical surface reconstructions. Morphometric measures, including sulcal length, depth, and cortical thickness, were extracted and normalized to hemisphere-wide variables. Between-group analyses tested whether PCGS presence, asymmetry, and quantitative morphology differed by diagnosis, while behavioral analyses examined associations with inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity, and cognitive measures. Age and gender were included as covariates. Results: Analyses revealed that, in both NT and ADHD individuals, there was significant leftward asymmetry in PCGS presence. Between groups, the PCGS was less likely to be present in individuals with ADHD in the left hemisphere. Leftward PCGS absence was also associated with significantly higher ADHD index and hyperactivity-impulsivity scores. Conclusions: These findings advance understanding of how early neurodevelopmental variation in cortical folding may serve as a structural intermediary between genetic liability and the behavioral expression of ADHD.

title: Lysosomal Glycosaminoglycan Catabolism Regulates Microglial Cell State in the Developing CNS
authors: Hope, K. T.; Zhang, Y.; Basu, A.; Luo, B.; Chassie, K.; Weiss, R. J.; Yellajoshyula, D.
abstract: Remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM), a complex structural and signaling network of the nervous system, is essential for CNS development, plasticity, and injury responses, yet how individual neural cell types contribute to this process remains poorly understood. Here, we show that phagocytic clearance of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), major components of the ECM, is an intrinsic function of microglia in the developing CNS. Our studies reveal an unexpected finding that impaired GAG clearance shifts microglia toward a non-homeostatic cell state seen in immature and disease-associated microglia (DAM), supporting a reciprocal relationship between the ECM and microglia. Using mouse models of Mucopolysaccharidosis VII, we examined the consequences of deleting {beta}-glucuronidase (GUSB), a lysosomal enzyme required for GAG degradation. Loss of GUSB causes early accumulation of undegraded chondroitin sulfate within microglial lysosomes, as confirmed by LC-MS analysis of intracellular GAGs isolated from cortical microglia. Single-cell RNA sequencing identified Gusb-null microglia as a distinct transcriptional population enriched for a core transcriptome shared by immature and disease-associated microglia. Together, these findings establish lysosomal GAG catabolism as a pathway that links ECM remodeling to the acquisition of adult homeostatic microglial identity during CNS development.

title: Oligodendrocyte stress response as a driver of vascular dementia
authors: Merour, E.; Ghatage, T.; Corbett, C.; DeBerge, M.; Kunjamma, R.; Ian Steckler, I. S.; Heidari, M.; Sorond, F. A.; Flanagan, M. E.; Thorp, E. B.; Popko, B.
abstract: Vascular dementia (VaD) is a prevalent and devastating neurocognitive disorder characterized by profound white matter damage, yet the precise cellular mechanisms linking cerebrovascular stress to demyelination remain poorly understood. Here, we characterize the impact of a chronic cardiometabolic stress regimen combining a high-fat diet and hypertension (HF/HBP) on central nervous system structure and function. Adult HF/HBP mice exhibit progressive oligodendroglial cell loss and myelin thinning, followed by cognitive impairments, anxiety-like behavior, and memory deficits that recapitulate clinical features of VaD. Mechanistically, we identify the integrated stress response (ISR) as a central driver of this pathology; pharmacological inhibition of the ISR restores myelination, while cell-specific genetic deletion of the ISR-activating kinase PERK from oligodendrocytes fully protects mice from HF/HBP-induced pathological and behavioral defects. Furthermore, we provide translational evidence that the ISR is activated in oligodendrocytes in human cases of cerebrovascular disease. Together, these findings reveal a critical, cell-autonomous role for oligodendroglial ISR activation during cerebrovascular stress and position this pathway as a viable therapeutic target to mitigate VaD pathogenesis.

title: High-throughput light-sheet 3D microscopy of whole rodent brain microstructure for integration with MRI
authors: Hanmer, J. M.; D'Antonio, F.; Manzano-Patron, J.-P.; Assimopoulos, S.; Wood, S. C.; Tachrount, M.; Shen, Q.; Craig, M.; Lai, C.; Hickman, G. J.; Radfar, E.; Chisholm, K. I.; Farr, T. D.; Jasanoff, A.; Hoerder-Suabedissen, A.; Molnar, Z.; Ligneul, C.; Tisca, C.; Jbabdi, S.; Howard, A. F. D.; Miller, K. L.; de Guzman, E.; Lerch, J. P.; Sotiropoulos, S. N.
abstract: Whole-brain cellular mapping is essential for understanding how differences in cellular architecture shape brain organisation and function. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) provides whole-brain coverage in humans and animal models but is only indirectly sensitive to cellular features. Integrating MRI with whole-brain microscopy is therefore critical for interpreting existing microstructural MRI metrics and developing new, more specific ones. Here, we present a scalable cross-resolution framework that integrates 3D light-sheet microscopy (LSM) of intact rodent brains with diffusion MRI (dMRI) to bridge cellular and macroscopic brain imaging. By combining active electrotransport-based tissue clearing and immunolabelling with accelerated LSM acquisitions, we achieve whole-brain multiplexed mapping of neuronal and glial populations in intact rodent brains on timescales comparable to conventional histology and 2D microscopy. This throughput enables LSM and MRI integration at scale, linking macroscopic MRI contrasts to microscopic cellular features within the same tissue. We apply this framework across eight genetically diverse mouse strains to develop predictive models of 3D microscopy-derived cellular features from multi-shell dMRI-derived contrasts. We demonstrate that data-driven combinations of state-of-the-art dMRI contrasts predict neuronal and astrocytic features better than individual contrasts, across all animals. Our novel approach enables 3D microscopy to guide the development and interpretation of microstructural MRI measures that are ultimately translatable to the living human brain.

title: VPS34 regulation in pulmonary arterial vascular smooth muscle cells in pulmonary hypertension
authors: Natoli, A.; Reinhard, B.; Hallee, L.; Zhang, H.; Piza-Taylor, K.; Aung, F.; Poznahovska, A.; Gleghorn, J. P.; Lucas, R.; DiVita, M.; Shen, Y.
abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is characterized by the hyperproliferative phenotype of pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cells (PAVSMCs) and extensive extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. Vacuolar protein sorting 34 (VPS34), a Class III Phosphatidylinositol-3 Kinase (PI3K), regulates cell proliferation, but its specific function in pulmonary vascular remodeling remains poorly understood. We aim to determine the role of VPS34 activation and regulation in PAVSMC proliferation, matrix deposition, and the progression of PAH. First, we found a marked decrease in the inhibitory phosphorylation of VPS34 at Ser164 (P-S164-VPS34), indicative of constitutive VPS34 activation, in remodeled pulmonary arteries (PAs) from human PAH patients and male mice exposed to Sugen/Hypoxia (SuHx). In human PAH PAVSMCs, siRNA-mediated knockdown of VPS34 or pharmacological inhibition via the selective inhibitor SAR405 significantly blunted cell proliferation and reduced the production of fibronectin, a major component of the remodeled ECM. Mechanistically, we found that Akt activation in PAH PAVSMCs promotes VPS34 activation; Protein Phosphatase 1 Catalytic Subunit Alpha is a potential effector in VPS34 activation; and active VPS34 led to the activation of the mTOR/S6 signaling pathway with tuberous sclerosis complex 2 downregulation. Finally, in vivo treatment with SAR405 attenuated right ventricular systolic pressure, right ventricular hypertrophy, and pulmonary vascular remodeling in SuHx mice, while concurrently decreasing vascular fibronectin deposition. Our study demonstrates that VPS34 activation, driven by an Akt-mediated loss of the inhibitory P-S164, is crucial in PAVSMC proliferation and fibrotic vascular remodeling in PAH. Targeting the VPS34 axis represents a promising anti-remodeling therapeutic strategy for the treatment of PAH. Keywords: Pulmonary arterial hypertension, vacuolar protein sorting 34, pulmonary vascular remodeling, pulmonary arterial vascular smooth muscle

title: Single-cell variant landscape of the human mitochondrial genome reveals cell type-specific functions and disease mechanisms
authors: Liu, C.; Peng, T.; Cen, Z.; Lu, P.; Potluri, P.; Hu, P.; Zhang, S.; Lott, M. T.; Widjaja, G.; Wallace, D. C.; Xing, Y.; Pei, L.
abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) heteroplasmy is a significant source of cellular genetic diversity and can cause disease yet its distribution and functional importance across different human cell types are poorly understood. Here we present scMOCHA (Single-Cell Mitochondrial Omics for Cellular Heteroplasmy Analysis), a scalable computational framework that resolves highconfidence, single-cell resolution mtDNA heteroplasmy directly from standard single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. Using this tool to interrogate publicly available scRNA-seq datasets from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and bone marrow (BM) uncovered the single-cell landscape of mtDNA single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) and heteroplasmy across ages in human hematopoietic cell types. PBMCs and BM share many inherited homoplasmic and highly heteroplasmic SNVs, whereas somatic SNVs are tissue- and cell type-specific and distributed across the mtDNA genome, suggesting that they arise largely stochastically. mtDNA replication error is a dominant force shaping homoplasmic variants, while oxidative stress potentially drives a significant portion of heteroplasmic and somatic mutations. Importantly, we discover previously unknown cell type-specific and human disease-associated mtDNA SNVs. By coupling mtDNA genotypes with matched single-cell nuclear transcriptomes and structural modeling, we uncover potential molecular mechanisms by which disease-associated mtDNA SNVs impact cellular processes such as inflammation and contribute to disease. Together, these findings define the single-cell variant landscape of the human mitochondrial genome and reveal previously unrecognized lineage- and disease-associated patterns of mtDNA variation in the human hematopoietic system.

title: Convergent genome evolution reveals shared routes to salt tolerance in flowering plants
abstract: Transitions to saline environments pose formidable challenges to plants, yet halophytism has evolved independently across many flowering plant lineages. We assembled a comparative angiosperm gene catalog of ~10 million protein-coding genes from 232 genomes spanning 55 families, with similar representation of halophytes and salt-sensitive relatives, to identify convergent genomic signatures of halophytism. Halophytes show remarkable convergence with recurrent genomic trends in salt-response genes, including lower copy numbers, higher basal expression, more constrained expression variation, distinct evolutionary rates, and independent positive selection on select genes at the same amino acid sites across multiple halophyte lineages. Crops and their wild halophytic relatives differ in gene family evolution, particularly in stress-response pathways. These findings reveal repeatedly tested evolutionary routes to halophytism and establish a genomic foundation for translating convergent adaptations into salt-tolerant crops.

title: Mid-Infrared Photothermal Imaging Unveils Altered Stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD) Activity in Ovarian Cancer Cells
authors: Teng, X.; Xia, T.; Yin, J.; Li, M.; Ao, J.; Ding, G.; Prabhu Dessai, C. V.; Isac, A. M.; Matei, D.; He, H.; Cheng, J.-X.
abstract: Stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD)-catalyzed fatty acid desaturation plays a key role in cancer metabolism reprogramming. While existing approaches enable quantification of SCD expression, directly monitoring in situ SCD enzymatic activity alterations remains challenging. Here, we report a strategy to measure intracellular SCD activity alterations and SCD product distributions by mid-infrared photothermal (MIP) imaging. Fully deuterated palmitic acid (PA-d31) is repurposed here as a chemical probe to report the SCD activity via a new peak at 2246 cm-1, corresponding to the stretching of D-C=C-D bonds in the SCD product. The MIP intensity ratio between the product-associated signal and the total C-D signal defines the apparent SCD activity index. By visualization of SCD-catalyzed metabolic conversion, our approach reveals altered SCD activity in cisplatin-treated ovarian cancer cells, ovarian cancer stem cells and cells fed with oleic acid. Non-uniform distributions of the SCD product are also observed. These results establish bio-orthogonal MIP microscopy as a platform for studying intracellular enzymatic reactions in living systems.

title: LOCALE: Local-Alignment Embeddings for Noise-Robust DNA Search at Scale
authors: Synk, R.; Pandey, P.; Sahinalp, C.; Duraiswami, R.
abstract: Searching petabase-scale repositories of raw sequencing data such as the NIH Sequence Read Archive (SRA) could unlock biological insights that remain inaccessible. Existing sequence-search methods either do not scale well or rely on exact $k$-mer matching that is brittle to genomic variation, which is high both within and across species and is further compounded by sequencing error. We recast sequence search as dense retrieval: we learn sequence embeddings whose inner-product similarity ranks locally aligned sequences above unaligned ones. We introduce LOCALE, an encoder trained with an InfoNCE objective on biologically informed augmentations: overlapping crops of parent sequences corrupted with substitutions, insertions, and deletions. This training recipe, rather than a specialized architecture, consistently induces variation-robust representations across four encoders spanning three tokenization schemes, improving Recall@$R_q$ by 7--39 points at 10% genomic variation. On a 50-accession SRA benchmark LOCALE retains 63.2% Recall@$R_q$ at 10% variation while existing k-mer indexes and DNA embedding methods fall below 35%, and on the full 4,571-accession MetaGraph benchmark (296 Gbp, 2.06 billion vectors) it achieves 4.5x the AUPRC of MetaGraph, the state-of-the-art k-mer index, with a single-node GPU IVF-PQ index retaining a 3.6x advantage at MetaGraph's query latency. Our encoder and training strategy generalize to real biological variance: on a cross-genotype Hepatitis B task, querying reads from one genotype against accessions of another with >8% natural divergence, LOCALE reaches 0.813 Recall@R_q versus 0.518 for MetaGraph.

title: AlphaFold3 and Intrinsically Disordered Proteins: Reliable Monomer Prediction, Unpredictable Multimer Performance
authors: Dao, T. M.; Ghent, S.; Uversky, V. N.; Rahman, T.
abstract: AlphaFold3 represents a major advance in protein structure prediction, yet its performance on intrinsically disordered proteins remains uncharacterized. We present the first systematic evaluation of AF3 on disordered systems, revealing a striking dichotomy. For monomers, AF3's pLDDT scores reliably predict disorder (MCC: 0.693), matching AlphaFold2 and rivaling dedicated predictors. This consistency across fundamentally different architectures confirms that disorder prediction emerges from training data, not model design. For multimers, the picture grows complex. Despite comparable aggregate performance (mean DockQ: 0.563 vs 0.571), AF3 and AF2 achieve these results through fundamentally different mechanisms. Conventional structural features explain 58% of AF2's variance but only 42% of AF3's. Users cannot predict when AF3 will succeed or fail from interface properties alone. On disorder-to-order transitions (MFIB benchmark), both models perform equally well, successfully predicting final folded states. Yet seed variance analysis reveals AF3's failures are deterministic: the model converges to identical structures across independent runs, whether correct or incorrect, indicating rigid structural priors override available information. Our findings establish AF3 as reliable for the prediction of monomer disorder but unpredictable for multimers. Architectural innovation alone cannot overcome training data bias. Progress demands disorder-enriched datasets and ensemble sampling, not merely novel architectures.

title: Imputing relative abundances via Gaussian random fields
authors: Shternshis, A.; Singh, P.; Hugerth, L. W.
abstract: Longitudinal studies with human participants frequently face the challenge of missing samples, which lead to incomplete trajectories of participant biomarkers and a reduction in data size. Existing approaches focus on single-variable imputation or model features one at a time, while neural networks typically require a large number of parameters and substantial training data. To address these challenges, we present an explainable model for multiple imputation of compositional samples based on a Gaussian random field (GRF). The model is specifically designed for longitudinal data: it incorporates participant-specific information and accounts for both temporal dependence across repeated observations and within-sample correlations, while using a moderate number of parameters. By coupling the GRF with sparse activation functions, the framework outputs sum-constrained compositions and explicitly models zero inflation. Under the Aitchison and Jensen--Shannon distances, our framework achieves imputation accuracy comparable to that of an observation-carrying baseline, while overcoming its static nature by modeling temporal trajectories and multivariate correlations. The resulting multiple imputations allow us to reconstruct complete datasets for downstream analysis and uncertainty quantification. We demonstrate the practical utility of our framework on gut microbiome datasets, restoring incomplete time series and achieving a balanced accuracy of 0.72 in predicting food allergy in infants (sensitivity 0.8) and of 0.64 in forecasting postpartum depression.
